title: What is operating leverage, and why do fixed costs make profit swing?
description: How fixed and variable costs shape profit, what operating leverage means, and how to use it in profitability and investment cases.
hook: Two businesses can have the same revenue and profit today, yet react completely differently when sales change. The reason is how their costs are built. Understanding fixed and variable costs is one of the most useful pieces of business intuition you can bring into a case.
body:
Fixed and variable, quickly

Fixed costs stay the same whatever the volume: rent, salaried staff, equipment, insurance. Variable costs rise with each unit sold: ingredients, packaging, delivery, sales commissions.

Operating leverage

A business with mostly fixed costs has high operating leverage. Once fixed costs are covered, almost every extra sale is profit, so a small rise in sales lifts profit sharply. The flip side: a small fall in sales hits profit hard. Airlines, hotels, cinemas and software companies are classic examples.

A simple illustration

Two companies both make £1 million revenue and £100,000 profit. Company A has £800,000 of fixed costs and £100,000 of variable costs. Company B is the other way round: £100,000 fixed and £800,000 variable.

  • Sales rise 10%. Company A's variable costs rise only £10,000, so profit almost doubles to £190,000. Company B's variable costs rise £80,000, so profit rises to £120,000, up 20%.
  • Sales fall 10%. Company A's profit drops to just £10,000, almost wiped out. Company B's falls to £80,000, down 20%.

Same revenue, same profit, very different risk.

Why it matters in a case

  • Profit cases: a small drop in volume can explain a big drop in profit in a high fixed-cost business. Check volume before hunting for rising costs.
  • Capacity and investment cases: filling empty capacity (seats, rooms, machine time) is very profitable, so ask about utilisation before building more.
  • Pricing: in high fixed-cost businesses, discounts to fill spare capacity can make sense, as long as price stays above variable cost.

A phrase to use

Since most of the cinema's costs are fixed, a 10% fall in attendance would hit profit far harder than 10%. I'd like to check volumes first.
